title: Negative nouns: palloa, kirjaa, autoa, kynää
summary: When possession is denied, the thing takes a noun form called the partitive. For the eight regular words used here, add -a or -ä to the whole basic word.
targetSkills: Regular singular partitive in negative possession
objectives: Form palloa, kirjaa, autoa, kynää, kissaa, koiraa, tyynyä, and peliä for negative possession.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: When possession is denied, the thing takes a noun form called the partitive. For the eight regular words used here, add -a or -ä to the whole basic word.

Back vowels a, o, u take -a; front vowels ä, ö, y take -ä. Neutral e and i do not override a back vowel. Pallo + -a = palloa; kirja + -a = kirjaa; auto + -a = autoa; kynä + -ä = kynää. Other noun types have other partitive rules.
These bounded regular nouns take -a with a, o, u and -ä with front vowels or only e, i. Peli becomes peliä; tyyny becomes tyynyä. This is not a rule for every Finnish noun ending in i.
keyPoints: Negative nouns: palloa, kirjaa, autoa, kynää
Use one singular thing and the owner form shown by the prompt.

sections.title: Regular noun forms in these examples
paragraphs: These forms name the thing after ei ole. The prompts show the noun form whenever forming it is outside this lesson’s target.
keyPoints: kissa (“cat”) → kissaa (“a cat”): regular singular partitive
koira (“dog”) → koiraa (“a dog”): regular singular partitive
tyyny (“pillow”) → tyynyä (“a pillow”): regular singular partitive
peli (“game”) → peliä (“a game”): regular singular partitive

examples.english: I do not have a ball.
steps: minulla means “I as the owner”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Pallo has back vowels a/o, so add -a: pallo + -a = palloa. Keep the final o before the ending.
Put palloa (“a ball”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: You do not have a book.
steps: sinulla means “you as the owner” for one person. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Kirja contains the back vowel a; neutral i does not override it. Add -a: kirja + -a = kirjaa, keeping both adjacent a vowels.
Put kirjaa (“a book”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: She does not have a dog.
steps: hänellä means “he as the owner” or “she as the owner”; this example uses “she”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Koira contains back vowels o/a and neutral i. Add -a: koira + -a = koiraa; the two final a vowels remain.
Put koiraa (“a dog”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: We do not have a car.
steps: meillä means “we as the owner”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Auto contains back vowels a/u/o. Add -a to the whole word: auto + -a = autoa.
Put autoa (“a car”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: You do not have a game.
steps: teillä means “you as the owner” for a group. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Peli has only neutral vowels e/i, so this taught regular noun uses -ä: peli + -ä = peliä. Other i-ending noun types have different rules.
Put peliä (“a game”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: They do not have a pen.
steps: heillä means “they as the owner”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Kynä has front vowels y/ä and no back vowel. Add -ä: kynä + -ä = kynää, keeping both adjacent ä vowels.
Put kynää (“a pen”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: I do not have a cat.
steps: minulla means “I as the owner”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Kissa has back vowel a despite neutral i. Add -a: kissa + -a = kissaa; keep both final a vowels.
Put kissaa (“a cat”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: We do not have a pillow.
steps: meillä means “we as the owner”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Tyyny has front vowel y and no back vowel. Add -ä: tyyny + -ä = tyynyä; keep the complete basic word before the ending.
Put tyynyä (“a pillow”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

commonMistakes: After ei ole, use the partitive noun, not its basic form: palloa, rather than pallo.
Keep the final vowel when adding the ending: kirja + -a = kirjaa and kynä + -ä = kynää.
Choose the ending from the noun: back vowels take -a; front or neutral-only vowels take -ä in these regular words, including peli → peliä.
